2. Further to the Application in Writ Petition No. 2669 of 2000 a Rule Nisi was issued with regard to the Rangamati, Khagrachari and Bandarban Hill District Local Government Council (Amendment) Acts 1998 (Acts Nos.  9, 10 and 11 of 1998) and the Chittagong Hill Tracts regional Council Act, 1998 (Act No. 12 of 1998) calling upon the Respondents to show cause as to why sections 3, 4(Kaka) and (Kha), 5, 6 (Uo), 7 and 11 of the Impugned Acts Nos. 9, 10 and 11 of 1998, section 15(Kha) of the Impugned Acts Nos.  9 and 10 and section 14(Kha) of the Impugned Act No. 11, section 28 of the Impugned Acts Nos. 9 and 10 of 1998 and section 27 of the Impugned Act No. 11 of 1998, section 29 of the Impugned Acts Nos. 9 and 10 of 1998 and section 28 of the Impugned Act No. 11 of 1998, section 31 of the Impugned Acts Nos. 9 and 10 of 1998 and section 30 of the Impugned Act No. 11 of 1998, section 34 of the Impugned Acts Nos. 9 and 10 of 1998 and section 33 of the Impugned Act No. 11 of 1998, section 25 of the Impugned Acts Nos. 9 and 10 of 1998 and section 24 of the Impugned Act No. 11, and sections 5(2), 5(8), section 7 and section 40 of the Impugned Act No. 12 of 1998, and sections 4(4) and 5(1) and (2) of Acts No. 19, 20 and 21 of 1989 should not be declared unconstitutional and, therefore, void and why the Regional Council Act of 1998 (Act No. 12 of 1998) should not be declared unconstitutional and, therefore, void or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. A further Rule Nisi issued in Writ Petition No. 2669 of 2000 calling upon the. Respondents to show cause as to why the impugned agreement dated 2 December 1997 (being the Chittagong Hill Tracts Peace Accord) signed by the Convener of the National Committee on Chittagong Hill Tracts ("NCCHT") and the Chairman of the Parbottyo Chattagram Jana Shanghati Samity ("PCJSS") (Annexure-B of the Writ Petition) should not be declared to have been made and executed without any lawful authority and contrary to the express provisions of the Constitution and, therefore, void and or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 3. In Writ Petition No. 6451 of 2007 a Rule Nisi was issued upon the. Respondents to show cause as to why the Parbottyo Chattagram Shand Chukti (Chittagong Hill Tracts Peace Accord), ,1997 (hereinafter interchangeably referred to as the ''CHT Peace Accord" or the "Peace Accord") signed and executed in the name of the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh with he PCJSS at Dhaka on 18 Agrahayan 1404 BS (2 December 1997), by violating the provisions of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and in contravention of the sovereignty of Bangladesh and the supremacy of it's sacred Constitution, should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect and/ or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit, and proper. 

 4. Keeping in view the sequentially of facts arising in these Applications, this Court deems it pertinent to first take up the matters at issue in Writ Petition No. 2669 of 2000. The Petitioner in this Writ Petition is a businessman aggrieved by the passing of the Rangamati, Khagra Chari and Bandarban Hill District Local Government Council (Amendment) Acts 1998 (Act Nos.  9, 10 and 11 of 1998) in that certain provisions of these Acts and the amendments introduced brought by them have affected his right of franchise, right to purchase and transfer property and the right to contest various elected posts. The Petitioner is further aggrieved by the provisions Of the Chittagong Hill Tracts Regional Council Act, 1998 (Act No. 12 of 1998) in that it has effectively created an autonomous .region being the Chittagong Hill Tracts ("CHT") by disgruntling the unitary character of Bangladesh. Asserting that the unitary character of the State constitutes the basic structure of the Constitution, the Petitioner submits that should such unitarily of the State be dismantled, that would strike at the very core of the Constitution causing it to be undeniably violated. 

 5. The CHT consisting of three districts, namely, Rangamati, Bandarban and Khagrachari covers a total area of 5,138 square miles which is one-tenth of the total territorial area of Bangladesh and is home to a population of about 10 Lac which constitutes 0.5% of the total population of Bangladesh. Topographically, the CHT is a distinctly hilly area dotted by valleys. An understanding of the history of the civil and political administration of the area now known as the CHT takes one back to the 18th century when in 1760 the then Mughal Governor of the province of Bengal transferred the then District of Chittagong to the British East India Company. A century later in 1860, the British colonial government formed the Chittagong Hill District comprising of the eastern hilly areas of the then Chittagong District. In 1900 important and far reaching changes in the administration of the Hill Tracts were made by the British Government by enacting the Chittagong Hill Tracts regulation 1900 (Regulation No. 1 of 1900) (hereinafter interchangeably referred to as the "CHT Regulation 1900" or the "Regulation") and by 'framing Rules there under. The Regulation, the Rules and Orders of the CHT came to be collectively known as the 'Hill Tracts Manual' in accordance with the provisions of which the CHT continued to be administered. 

 6. Pursuant to the Hill Tracts Manual the CHT came to be divided into three circles, namely, the Chakma Circle with headquarters at Rangamati, the Bomang Circle with headquarters at Bandarban, and the Mong Circle with headquarters at Manik Chari in Khagrachari. The head of the Circle is known as the Chief, popularly known as the 'Raja' or 'King'. These Circle Chiefs or Kings have always had a distinctive role to play in the administration of the CHT notwithstanding that the administration was formally run by the Deputy Commissioners and Sub-divisional Deputy Commissioners. Notably, though the CHT fell within the boundaries of the undivided province of Bengal, its administration by different law as reflected in the Hill Tracts Manual led it to acquire the status of a 'Non-regulated District'. 

 7. By section 5 read with section 46(1) of the Government of India Act 1935, ("the 1935 Act") Bengal was a Governor's province in the Federation of India. Section 91(1) of the 1935 Act empowered the King by Order in Council to declare certain areas as "excluded area" and "partially excluded area." By section 2, read with Part I of the Schedule to the Government of India (Excluded and Partially Excluded Areas) Order 1936, the 'Chittagong Hill Tracts' under the province of Bengal was specified as an excluded area. By section 92 of the 1935 Act, though the executive authority of a province extended to excluded and partially excluded areas, the provision nevertheless was against the application of any Act of the Federal or Provincial Legislature, "to an excluded or partially excluded area unless the Governor by public notification so directs." 

 8. The Indian Independence Act 1947, ("the 1947 Act"), enacted by the British Parliament on 18 July 1947 and creating the two independent dominions namely India and Pakistan with effect from 15 August 1947, by section 2 specified the territories of the two dominions. Accordingly, by operation of section 3 of the 1947 Act the province of Bengal as constituted under the 1935 Act ceased to exist, and two new provinces known as East Bengal and West Bengal were constituted. It is to be noted that in the First Schedule to the 1947 Act, which provisionally included the Bengal districts in the new province of East Bengal, the Chittagong Hill District was conspicuously absent. Such absence finds meaning and substance in the provisions of section 8 of the 1947 Act, by virtue of which the 1935 Act continued, with necessary amendments, to be the Constitution of Pakistan until March 1956 when the first Constitution of Pakistan was framed. Consequently, by operation of section 5 read with sections 46(1), 91 and 92 of the amended Government of India Act 1935 (as amended by the Constituent Assembly of Pakistan from time to time) the position of the CHT as an excluded area in the province of East Bengal remained unaltered. 

 (d) A constitutional provision restricting the amendment of the CHT Regulation 1900, and imposing a ban on Bengali settlement in the CHT. It is averred that these demands were rejected outright by the Prime Minister who, on the contrary, argued for relinquishing such parochial and ethnic aspirations in favour of these being subsumed under a broader notion of nationalism to facilitate national integration. 

 11. This is the political and constitutional backdrop against which Mr MN Larma as a member of the Constituent Assembly, in a display of his rejection of this unitary character of the State is shown to have refused to vote for the new Constitution as adopted in November 1972. It is noted that a political mobilization of the tribal peoples had by then been already underway as evident in the formation in early 1972 of the PCJSS as a political front with Mr MN Larma at the helm. Consequently, the Shanti Bahini, an armed wing of the PCJSS was formed on 7 January 1973 that, after the assassination of Prime Minister Sheikh Mujibur Rahman in August 1975 became a clandestine organization engaged in armed insurgency against the Government. 

 12. This Court notes that subsequent developments in the CHT and the political positioning of the PCJSS along with the Shanti Bahini vis-a-vis successive governments came to be greatly informed by the taxonomy of citizen-ship as adopted in the 1972 Constitution in reinforcement of the unitary character of the new State. The Constitution as adopted in November 1972 having termed every citizen as "Bangalee" (Bengali), MN Larma could be said to have drawn the battle lines very early on in 1972 when he vehemently opposed on the floors of the Constituent Assembly the lumping together of the Chakma people with Bengalis in blatant disregard of the Chakmas' separate identity. The seed of the unitarily of the State so sown in the Constitution is perhaps nowhere better manifested than in the Bengali immigration into the CHT in the following decades. A succinct account of the various phases of such migration considered in their larger historical context is found in Devasish Roy's chapter entitled "The Discordant Accord: Challenges In The Implementation of the Chittagong Hill Tracts Accord of 1997" in "Implementing Negotiated Agreements: The Real Challenge to Intrastate peace," edited by Miek Boltjes at pages 115-146 (TMC Asser Press, the Haque, Netherlands, 2007) Mr Roy writes accordingly at pages 121-122: 

 "Bengali in-migration into the CHT had started during the nineteenth century, but even after the departure of the British in 1947, the settlers name up less than 10 percent of the population. This was to rise to almost 50 percent in 1991, making the indigenous people a near-minority in their ancestral homeland. The internal immigration policies of the different governments were not the same. The British government had allowed limited immigration into the CHT in order to facilitate trade and irrigation-oriented intensive agriculture, both the which were relatively new to the indigenous peoples. It was careful not to allow large-scale immigration, fearing the growth of anti-British sentiments, which were more common in the plains of Bengal. The Pakistani government's role (1947-1971) regarding immigration was more ambivalent, while the role of successive Bangladeshi administrations on this issue has varied from covert encouragement (early 1970s) to a directly sponsored population transfer programme (1979 to 1984). The transmigration of the largely Muslim peasants from various lowland districts led to the displacement of tens of thousands of indigenous people, thereby partly civilianizing the ongoing conflict and adding ethnic and religious overtones to a conflict that was hitherto largely restricted to the non-Muslim indigenous guerrillas and predominantly Muslim Bengali government security forces. Of course, that does not mean that innocent civilians, whether Bengali or indigenous, were not victimized earlier, but at least their number until then was not so visibly large. This part-civil part-military conflict continued up to the 1990s and it was not until the signing of the 1997 Accord that the organized internal war formally ended. In the meantime, thousands of lives had been lost, tens or thousands of people rendered homeless, and an untold number had to suffer the indignities of rape, torture and imprisonment. Although there were casualties on both sides of the ethnic divide, the indigenous people suffered the most because the balance of force was not on their side, among other things. Moreover, the security forces had, on the whole, paid little heed towards the human rights of the indigenous people in their quest to contain the insurgency." 

 13. It is against the backdrop of such a "part-civil part-military conflict" in the CHT that on 6 March 1989 three identical laws, namely Rangamati Hill District Local Government Council Act 1989 (Act No. 19 of 1989) Khagrachari Hill District Local Government Council Act 1989 (Act No. 20 of 1989) and Bandarban Hill District Local Government Council Act 1989 (Act No. 21 of 1989) (hereinafter collectively referred to as "the Original Acts of 1989" as necessary) were passed by Parliament by which local governments were established in the three Hill Districts under Article 59 of the Constitution. These laws made detailed provisions for the establishment and functioning of local governments by the elected representatives of the people consisting of both the tribal people and Bengali settlers. The political context, necessity and objective of these three pieces of legislation is explained in Moudud Ahmed's book titled "South Asia: Crisis of Development—The Case of Bangladesh" (The University Press Limited, Dhaka 2002) at pages 64-65 thus: 

 "When Ershad finally realised that the military option would not work, he made serious attempts to arrive at a political solution. A high-powered national committee, headed by Air Vice Marshal (Red) AK Khandaker assisted by the Area Commanding Officer General Abdus Salam, entered into protracted negotiations with the belligerent leaders, which continued for about eighteen months. The two sides arrived at a consensus and a written understanding was drawn up on how to bring about a structural change for maximum self-rule within the framework of a sovereign Bangladesh. The arrangement enabled the tribesmen to retain their own culture and heritage and at the same time to look after their own administrative affairs. This understanding was then codified, with the approval of the cabinet, into three separate laws enacted for the local governments at Rangamati, Bandarban and Khagrachari districts. 

 The scheme was to have a 31-member Local Government Council in each district, the Chairman and Members of which would be directly elected by the people in such a manner that both the tribes and settlers would be represented in proportion to their population but under all circumstances the Chairman and the majority Members would be from among the tribesmen. Besides education, health, agriculture, livestock and other subjects, the two most crucial areas for the tribesmen to retain control, were the right to land and law and order. The tribesmen were very sensitive about their land being taken over by outsiders by purchase or lease, and their internal security system failing to provide adequate guarantee for their safety. The law provided that no land in the district could charge hands without the authority of the elected council, all the personnel up to the level of Sub-Inspector of Police would be recruited locally, and the police would function under the control of the Council. 

 14. Therefore, as part of and in evidence of the latest phase in a political arrangement or exercise to restore peace in the CHT, on 2 December 1997 the CHT Peace Accord was signed between the NCCHT formed by the Government of Bangladesh and the PCJSS. While on behalf of the Government of Bangladesh Mr Abul Hasnat Abdullah signed the Peace Accord in his capacity as the NCCHT, Mr Joytirindra Bodhipriya, otherwise known as Santu Larma, signed the peace Accord in his capacity as the Chairman, PCJSS. 

 15. The Petitioners in both these Applications now submit that Mr Abul Hasnat Abdullah had no authority under the Constitution to sign the Peace Accord on behalf of the Government of Bangladesh. Furthermore, in dwelling on the legislation stemming from the CHT Peace Accord, the Petitioner in Writ Petition No. 2669 of 2000 refers to the three identical laws namely the Rangamati Hill District Local Government Council (Amendment) At 1998, (Act 9 of 1998), Khagrachari Hill District Local Government Council (Amendment) Act 1998 (Act 10 of 1998), and Bandarban Hill District Local Government Council (Amendment) Act 1998 (Act 11 of 1998) (hereinafter referred to as "the Impugned Acts") as passed by Parliament on 24 May 1998 with a view to amending certain provisions of the Original Acts of 1989 (Acts Nos. 19, 20 and 21 of 1989). On 3 December 1998, section 2 (Ka Ka) of the Impugned Act have been further amended by which a non-tribal permanent resident would now mean a person who is the owner of lawful land and also has a permanent address in a Hill District. 

 16. Apprehending that the Peace Accord coupled with the legislations has spurred effectively create a "parallel government" or "a state within a state" based on misconceived notions of determining the extent of backwardness of the tribal peoples of the CHT, the following submissions on the Impugned. Acts are accordingly made by the Petitioner: 

 i. 	By sections, 2, 3, 4(Kha), 5, 6 and 7 of the Impugned Acts, the deletion of the words "Local Government" from the long title and from section 1(1), 2(Uo), 3 and 7 of the three Original Acts of 1989, have prima facie taken the Rangamati, Khagrachari and Bandarban administrative units outside the purview of Local Government enunciated in Part IV, Chapter-III of the Constitution and is, therefore, violative of Articles 1, 7, 59 and 60 of the Constitution. 

 iv. 	Section 28 of the Impugned Acts Nos.  9 and 10 and section 27 of the Impugned Act No. 11 as amends section 62 of the Original Acts by which permanent preference has been ensured in the Police Service for the tribal people, such preference being discriminatory against the Bengali settlers, therefore, violates the guarantees under Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. 

 vi. 	The new section 67 of the Original Acts as brought about by section 31 of the Impugned Acts Nos.  9 and 10, and. section 30 of the Impugned Act No. 11, which provides that if coordination is needed in the discharge of functions of the Government of Bangladesh and the Council, each party can give specific proposal to the order and an agreement can be reached through mutual consultation and discussion, is violative of Articles 1, 7(1) and 55(2) of the Constitution inasmuch as his section brings the Council at part with the Executive Government of the country which is against the concept of unitary Government. 

 vii. 	The repeal of section 70 from the Original Acts by virtue of section 34 of the Impugned Acts Nos. 9 and 10 and section 33 of Impugned Act No. 11 by which the Government's power of delegation of its functions under the act to any functionary has been abolished, has put a fetter on the normal functioning of the executive Government and is, therefore, unlawful and unconstitutional. 

 viii. 	The repeal of sections 51 and 52 from the Original Acts of 1989 by virtue of section 25 of the Impugned Acts Nos. 9 and 10 of 1998 and section 24 of the Impugned Act No. 11 of 1998 by which the central Government's power of control over, and investigation into, the functions of the District Councils have been abolished is violative of Article 1, 7(1), 55(2) of the Constitution. 

 18. The Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs and the Cabinet Division as Respondent No. 1 respectively in both Writ Petitions in defending the peace process has submitted that the CHT Peace Accord was signed and executed in 1997 to facilitate the public interest in general, and specially for the people living in the CHT, in order to bring back peace and harmony in the said region of Bangladesh so that tribal and non-tribal living in that area may co-exist there. The objectives of the peace process have also been significantly to give effect to a constitutional mandate for the advancement of backward sections of the population and the establishment of efficient local government institutions. Challenges mounted in these two Applications to the Peace Accord itself are seen by the Respondents as involving political and disputed questions of facts and as such not permitting of review by this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution given, primarily, that the Petitioners purport to challenge the execution, signing and implementation of the CHT Peace Accord, which is an agreement concerning the then political situation in the CHT, and as such under the settled principles of law, this Court or any other Court shall steer clear of any interference with or any determination of any such political settlement or question. It is emphasized in this regard by the said Respondents, that the Peace Accord is in the nature of a political agreement or memorandum of settlement entered into and executed in pursuance of the policy of the Government to restore peace, normalcy and stability in the CHT though the promotion of local government institutions in the CHT as provided in Articles 9, 11 and 14 of the Constitution. Furthermore, it is submitted that the signing of an, agreement as this does not have to satisfy the requirements of Article 145(1) of the Constitution which concerns contracts and deeds made in exercise of the executive authority of the Republic and which alone are required to be expressed to be made in the name of the President. It is explained that it is the usual practice for governments to adopt political policies for good governance, and in the case of the CHT too, the Government undertook a policy decision to bring back peace and stability to a part of the country that has suffered political unrest, ethnic conflict and insurgency for more than two decades sapping the resources of the country. Agreements of this nature are also submitted to be common in many countries of the world, and cited in this regard are, for example, the Mizoram Accord, 1985 (India), the Darjeeling Accord, 1988 (India), the Mindanao Accord, 1996 (Philippines), the Aceh Accord, 2002 (Indonesia), and the Northern Ireland Peace Accord, 1998 (UK), among others. 

 19. The plea on behalf of the Respondents in also for this Court to see the CHT Peace Accord in its proper historical context as but the latest stage or link in a long-standing peace initiative subscribed to and nurtured, albeit in varying degrees and varied results, by political regimes of all complexions. In that context it is highlighted that since 1976, in particular, the situation in the CHT deteriorated, and violence degenerated into insurgency, which was met by the deployment of military and paramilitary force in the CHT. That notwithstanding, it is also asserted that various governments continued to engage the PCJSS in active negotiations. Negotiations in the 1980s are shown in particular to have led to two agreements being signed with tribal leaders. One such agreement was signed in 1985, in which the Government was represented by Major General Nuruddin, GOC, 24 Infantry Division; Chittagong, while the PCJSS was represented, among others, by one Hari Kishto Chakma alias. Major Bidyut. Another agreement was signed in 1988 in which the Government was represented by Air Vice-Marshal AK Khandaker, then .Minister of Planning and head of the NCCHT, .while the tribal representatives included the Late Shantimoy. Dewan and others. It is on the basis of the letter agreement that the Local Government Council Acts of 1989 (since renamed the Hill District Council Acts of 1989) were passed. It is pointed out that the succeeding BNP-led government also formed a committee headed by Colonel Oli Ahmed, then Minister of Communications, which held several rounds of talks with the PCJSS leaders but failed to reach and agreement. It was only after this that the succeeding Awami League-led government reconstituted the NCCHT under the Chief Whip, Mr Abul Hasnat Abdullah, which finally led to the signing of the Peace Accord in 1997. 

 22. Drawing on an observation of the Court in Indra Sawhney vs Union of India reported in AIR 1993 (SC) 477 this Court cannot but help observe at the outset that the facts and issues raised in these two Writ Petitions place certain complex political, legal and constitutional questions for our consideration and determination and from which have stemmed, evidently, deeply entrenched political positions which could be or ought to have been settled more satisfactorily through an integrated political process based on a broad consensus at the initiative and behest of the elected branches of the Government. But that has not been done and the issues have been left to fester for far too long. The Judiciary has, therefore, had to step into a peace process in which the Executive and the Legislature still have a fair share of their responsibility to discharge. It shall be prudent at this juncture to point out, and as will be evident from the findings and observations hereinafter, that this Court having so stepped into that stagnant peace process shall necessarily have to guide the elected organs of the State through certain pathways to be pursued to revive or resuscitate the peace process with a view to its fruitful culmination. In that exercise this Court is mindful, however, of the limits on its ability to make comprehensive, detailed and specific prescriptions which must remain with-in the domain of authority of the elected law-givers and policy makers. This Court is altered to the pitfalls of doing otherwise by Justice Sandra Day O'Connor who, musing on her experiences in US Supreme Court in "The Majesty of The Law: Reflections of a Supreme Court Justice (Random House, 2003) writes at page 247: 

 23. The political context of these two Applications in the terms of what this Court perceives to be the political vicissitudes of the tribunal peoples is best introduced by the following excerpts from the Memoirs of the former Chakma Chief, Raja Tridiv Roy entitled "The departed Melody" (PPA Publications, Islamabad, Pakistan, July 2003) that provides an account of the post-1972 political developments bearing upon the CHT, the resultant conflict and the need to a political settlement as embodied in the Peace Accord. Raja Tridiv Roy appears to emphasize that Bengali nationalism in all its manifestations as informed post 1971 State formation and nation building by its very ethos remained so very exclusionary of other identities that the tribal peoples of CHT got political short-changed and became constitutional outcasts. In a chapter entitled "Traumas of the Chakmas", Raja Tridiv Roy writes thus at pages 330-331: 

 "Mahfuzul Hoque in "Ethnic Insurgency and National Integration" writes on page 80, "Misunderstanding between the Bangladesh Government and the tribal people arose immediately after independence. Bengali Freedom Fighters killed tribal people of Khagrachari, Dighinala and Barkal." And on page 81, "Widespread repression and atrocities during Mujib regime were committed by Rakkhi Bahini [paramilitary security force of the post-independent government] against the tribal people. And again he says, "At a rally at Rangamati Sheikh Mujib declared that all tribal people would be known as Bengali and would have no other identity." 

 In point of fact the Central and Provincial Legislatures had never before exercised any jurisdiction over the High Tracts until 1954. Before India was partitioned the Hill Tracts had been an Excluded Area and in the Pakistan Constitution of 1956 also it remained an Excluded Area and in the 1962 Constitution it retained its separate status as a Tribal Area. According to the rules the Chiefs formed the government's Advisory Council and they had to be consulted on all-important matters affecting the Hill Tracts. Despite Manabendra Narayan Larrna's eloquent pleadings in the Bangladesh Parliament, no constitutional safeguards were provided in the new Constitution, Larma led a delegation to Sheikh Mujib on 15 February 1972, with four demands including the retention of the Chittagong Hill Tracts regulation 1900, and special laws, but his demands were rejected. His plea for there tention of the powers of the Chiefs was accepted but in practice their advice was disregarded unless it coincided with government's particular interests. 

 Encountering only rejection from the Bangladesh leadership and Parliament, and as a consequence of Mujib's public utterance denying even their ethnic identities, the indigenous people were even more hurt and angered. Predictably the Awami League candidates were defeated in the parliamentary elections, having failed to acquire constitutional safeguards, facing renewed onslaughts on their culture and on their lands, the various indigenous peoples under the leadership of the Larma brothers formed the PCJSS Party on 7 March 1972 and later on 7 January 1973 the Shanti Bahini (Peace Force). The oppression and violence increased and the Jumma hill people realized that cultural and even physical extinction as a people was inevitable, and not in the distant but in the immediate future. The Larma brothers went under-ground. They had no option. To defend themselves the people launched the guerrilla war against the Bangladesh government. 

 On orders from the Ziaur Rahman government the directives that were issued by the Commissioner to Deputy Commissioners of the Chittagong Division marked "secret," were at first denied by the then Government of Bangladesh, and even the existence of such a policy. However, such a large transfer of population could not be hidden from the world at large. When confronted with the evidence, the government had no word of explanation, nor one of contrition. This gross attempt to forcibly appropriate their lands and drive away the indigenous Jumma people, and thereby to change the demographic composition of the Hill Tracts by converting the over-whelming majority population into a minority, demonstrates a mediaeval mindset similar to those of the fascists whose atrocities have shamed all mankind in the not too distant past. 

 During Pakistan days there was no government sponsored induction or infiltration by plainsmen. Mahfuzul Haque in "Ethnic Insurgency and National Integration," says: "In mid-1979 late President Ziaur Rahman took decision to settle land-less families in the sparsely populated areas of the hills. The decision was construed by the tribal leaders as a government attempt to change population pattern of the hills. In February, 1980, truckloads of poor Bengali families mainly from northern Bangladesh poured into the Hill Tracts. They were attracted by the government scheme to provide five acres of hilly laud, four acres of mixed lands, and 2.5 acres of paddy land for each newly settled Bengali family." 

 24. It is also to be noted at the outset that legal questions involved in these Applications will invariably involve the reference to the CHT Regulation 1900 and the present status of the various Writ Petitions and an appeal awaiting consideration by the High Court Division and the Appellate Division respectively in which the validity and the currency of the CHT Regulation 1900 is the focal issue. It shall suffice to note at this juncture that in the case of Rangamati Food Products Ltd vs Commission of Customs reported in 10 BLC 525 this Court, while discussing the question of the applicability of tax laws to the CHT, declared that the CHT Regulation 1900 is a "dead law". This led to the Government of Bangladesh to file Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 696 of 2006 against that particular portion of the judgment that has since resulted in a leave granted on 15 November 2007 to file the appeal. The operation of the judgment and order in the Rangamati Food Products Ltd. Case So far as it relates to the CHT Regulation 1900 has been stayed till the hearing of the appeal. This Court is informed by the Assistant Attorney General Mr Pratikar Chakma that the said appeal proceedings are yet to commence. 

 25. This judgment in the Rangamati Food Products Ltd Case finding on the CHT Regulation 1900 however runs in the face of several other judgments of the High Court in which the regulation has been accepted as valid and current. These cases include : Mustafa Ansari vs DC, CHT 7 DLR, 553, Collector of Central Excise & Land Customs vs Azizuddin Industries Ltd (23 DLR SC, 73), Shewe Hla Prue TK vs Commissioner Chittagong 44 DLR, 539, Aung Shwe Prue Chowdhury vs Kyaw Sain Prue Chowdhury 50 DLR, (AD) 73, Sainpriti Chakma vs Commissioner of Customs 5 BLC (AD) 29, Bikram Kishore Chakma vs Land Appeal Board 6 BLC 436, BFIDC vs Sheikh Abdul Jabbar 53 DLR 488, Abu Taher vs Land Appeal Board 8 BLC, 453, and Rajkumari Unika Devi vs Bangladesh 9 BLC, (AD) 181. This provided the context for the constitution of a Special Bench for hearing three Writ Petitions being Writ Petition No. 9513 of 2005 (SP Manna vs Deputy Commissioner, Rangamati and others), Writ Petition No. 3686 of 2004 (Anil Kanti Chakma vs Additional Divisional Commissioner, Chittagong and Others) and Writ Petition No. 149 of 2003 (Ulha Su Pru Chowlhuri vs Anaram Tripura) in which the question of the validity of this Regulation is moot. However, it appears now that the Special Bench having adjourned hearing on these three Writ Petitions in 2006 pending the outcome of CPLA No. 696 of 2006, the Appellate Division's. Order of 15 November 2007 will have pushed back further the prospects of the resumption of the Special Bench's proceedings. In that regard, this Court, therefore, deemed it prudent not to presently deal with the CHT Regulation 1900 substantively. It is noted, however, that both the CHT Peace Accord and the regional Council Act provide that the Regional Council shall advise the Government of Bangladesh to remove inconsistencies between the CHT Regulation 1900 and the three Hill Tract Council Acts of 1989. In this regard, it is the considered view of this Court that pursuant to the above referred Order of the Appellate Division of 15 November 2007 in CPLA No. 696 of 2006 a filing and disposal of the relevant appeal should advisedly be pursued actively by the Government for a final determination on the validity of the CHT Regulation 1900. A final determination of this particular appeal and of the other Writ Petitions which were to be heard and disposed of by the Special Bench of this Court pertaining to the CHT and the validity of the Regulation must, in our opinion, figure prominently and provide a fundamental legal basis in the Government's continued efforts to ensure a sustainable peace process in the CHT. 

 27. The material on record undoubtedly in the eyes of this Court establish that the Peace accord is but an intermediate state in a political process that commenced many years prior to 1997 and is in fact an ongoing one. It is also evident that by the execution of the Peace Accord an immediate political objective was achieved. That is, at a crucial period in Bangladesh's political history the Peace Accord of 1997 served to preserve this country's territorial integrity and sovereignty. It is, however, the longer term objective of the Peace Accord to secure autonomy in the CHT that is a more disputed matter. It is here that an assertion has been made on behalf of the Respondents to justify the Peace Accord as a mechanism clearly envisaged under Articles 28(4) and 29(3) of the Constitution to secure such autonomy for a backward section of the citizenry. In the course of his submissions on behalf of the Respondent Regional Council in both the Applications, Mr Devasish Roy has brought on record available statistics culled from varied sources that, he submits, manifestly establish that the tribal population in the CHT constitutes a backward section within the meaning of Articles 28(4) and 29(3) of the Constitution. Mr Roy has pointed out that the Government has identified certain indicators for determining backwardness of a section of the population, as evident in the Summary dated 14-10-2008 prepared by the Ministry of Chittagong Hill Tracts affairs for the consideration of the Chief Advisor to the Caretaker Government. These indicators include (1) communication; (2) non-agricultural land; (3) education; (4) electrification; (5) health and sanitation; (6) safe drinking water; (7) annual per capita income; and (8) availability of plain land. Mr Roy has submitted that the following, amongst others, statistics and data indicate that the tribal population of the CHT constitutes a backward section of our society: 

 ii.	Health : Except the Chakma, the Other tribes' access to sanitary latrine is very low compared to the Bengali population 50% of Bengalis have access to latrine compared to 29% Marma, 10.8% Tripura, 13.2% Bawm, 9.1% Mro, and 8.0% Tanchangya. Knowledge about symptoms of diarrhoea is 68% amongst the Bengali population compared to 65% in indigenous people. Only 34% of the indigenous population knows how to prepare oral re-hydration saline compared to 65% of Bengali people. Knowledge about vaccination of children is 37.7% in the Bengali population, compared to 22.2% indigenous people. In case of pregnancy care, only 9.5% indigenous people get antenatal care compared to 29.2% of Bengalis. 73.6% of Bengalis receive immunization during pregnancy, which is only 37.9% in case of indigenous people 8.2% Bengalis have postnatal care, compared to only 3% indigenous people. 

 iii.	Safe Drinking Water: Compared to 60% of Bengali people, only 36% of indigenous peoples in CHT use tubewell as source of drinking water. Only 33% of indigenous people use tube well as the source of cooking water compared to 42% Bengalis.  iv.	Electrification: About 91% indigenous households and 73% Bengali house-holds are deprived of electricity. 

 v.	Communication: The CHT tribes live in the remoter areas of the CHT compared to their Bengali counterparts. More than 10% of all Unions in the CHT (all situated in Baghaichhari, Juraichhari, Rowangchhari, Ruma and Thanchi thanas) are not accessible otherwise than by a travel on foot taking one or two days walking from the nearest road or riverside. These Unions are almost exclusively populated by the indigenous people. 

 28. The significance of the information and data produced by Mr Roy cannot indeed be underestimated. Nor can it be denied that the backwardness that such information attests to in all probability justifies measures as may be adopted exceptionally by the Government, as need be, under Articles 28(4) and 39(3) of the Constitution. But it is also clear to this Court that such provisions and mechanisms of affirmative action based on the notion of positive discrimination must also be measured against the standards enshrined in Articles 26, 27 and 31 of the Constitution and a concept of autonomy that deters active discriminatory of others. Writing on 'Democrati Autonomy' David Held in "Models of Democracy" (2nd Edition, Stanford University Press, Stanford California, 1996) explains that the appeal of democracy, especially in a truly pluralistic socio-political setting is its ability "to offer a basis for tolerating and negotiating difference "page, 297). That justifies the subscription to a concept of "autonomy" which, in this Court's opinion, should be the yardstick to determine the Nikes of the impugned legislation in particular. It is evident to this Court that the Peace Accord in fact regress Bangladesh's political circumstance as one constituted, to apply David Helds tests, by "plurality of identities, cultural forms and interests," which, therefore, allow Bangladesh's political culture to offer itself as a basis for "negotiating difference". Proceeding on that premise that the Peace Accord can be seen as providing political formulae for the creation of the best circumstance for the peoples of the CHT as a whole "to develop their natule and express their diverse qualities", "protecting from the arbitrary use of political authority and coercive power", "involvement of citizens in the determination of the conditions of their association" and "expansion of economic opportunity", these are aspirations that Held identifies as essential constituents of democratic autonomy with "autonomy" connoting the capacity of people to "to be self-determining" (Ibid, page 300). But fundamental to the operation of such a principle of autonomy is the notion that rights have a structural dimension bestowing opportunities and imposing duties. In other words, all citizens enjoy rights subject of and qualified by the rights of others. That is the core thesis of the "principle of autonomy" that has been enunciated thus: 

 29. It is in this context that it is noted that much of what was anticipated and stipulated in the multi-dimensional, multilayered Peace Accord has been translated into legislative action producing the four piece of impugned legislation. In this Court's view these Impugned Acts more aptly constitute the subject matter of judicial scrutiny. There are other provisions in the intricately stranded Peace Accord that are admittedly in the process of being implemented. Upon a consideration of the same it is evident that certain administrative, political and legal pathways are yet to evolve or be followed to fully implement these provisions. The pursuit of those pathways, particularly with regard to the effective functioning of the Land Commission, as are yet to be fully developed are not ripe understandably for constitutional scrutiny. The Peace Accord in this sense in indicative of future courses of action over and beyond the fulfillment of its primary objective of securing a political resolution to a politico-military conflict. Again, a resolution of the conflict itself, this Court finds, has inevitably led to an exhaustion of the Peace Accord's essential political substratum. It is in that overall context that we have considered the argument on behalf of the Respondent Regional Council by learned Advocate Dr. Kamal Hossain that the Peace Accord not amenable to a constitutional analysis adopting a strict constructionist approach. To the extent that the immediate political objectives of the Pea Ce Accord have been satisfied it is the Court's view that the Peace Accord does not indeed permit a judicial review at this point in time that is not to say, however, that political act are not per se amenable to judicial scrutiny. They are indeed so subject to such scrutiny should they involve constitutional is shall be seen the impugned legislation stemming from that Peace Accord and with which the relevant provisions of the Peace Accord can be said to have otherwise merged have indeed been accepted by this Court for independent judicial inspection below. This Court is also not inclined to accept the argument of the Respondents that since the laws in question were passed in 1998, that is subsequent to the Peace Accord and, since no government has proceeded on the premise that this is an unconstitutional Accord as evident in the absence of any issue to that effect having ever been raised in Parliament since 1997, and six successive governments having not repealed the Peace Accord, such delay and acceptance over a protracted period would obviate a judicial scrutiny of the Accord. That fact that such an argument is inherently misconceived is borne out by the judgment in the Italian Marble Case commonly known as the 5th Amendment Case reported in 2006 (Special Issue) BLT in which the 5the Amendment 1979 to the Constitution was revisited years later by the High Court Division as per a challenge made in December 2000 and the Rule made absolute in 2005. There are, however, certain features fundamental and unique to the Peace Accord itself that in this Court's perception takes it out of the fold of the constitutional scheme as we understand it. That Court has probed into this aspect in relation to the issue of the constitutionality of the execution of the Peace Accord raised by the Petitioner in both Writ Petitions. This Court in accepting the fact of political exigency that informed the adoption of a particular manner of execution of that Peace Accord notes that such mode of execution was informed in turn to a large extent of the parties' understanding of what was being executed. This Court is of the view that the Peace Accord is fundamentally an intrastate political pact that marks the cessation of hostilities between belligerents. At its core the multistanded Peace Accord is actually a 'Treaty of Peace' that proceeds beyond a mere truce and a mere true and aims at a permanent end to an insurgency based on commitments of sustainable peace. The Black's Law Dictionary defines such a 'treaty' to be an agreement of a contract made by belligerent powers, in which they agree to lay down their arms, and by which they stipulate the conditions of peace and regulate the manner in which it is to be restored and supported. In this Court's opinion, there is no better way to describe the Peace Accord. That being the case, the Peace Accord does not in this Court's opinion neatly fall into the category of Article 145 contracts and deeds or indeed Article 145A international treaties. It is clearly not a treaty as not being entered into between independent entities or communities having the right of self-government on account of one party to the Peace Accord, that is, the PCJSS not possessing such right of self-government. Though clearly not creating any obligation under international law the Peace Accord has on the other hand given rise to commitments. But stretching the interpretation of the Peace Accord has on the other hand given rise to commitments. But stretching the interpretation of the Peace Accord beyond that to bring it within the purview of Article 145 becomes problematic because Article 145 primarily deals with contracts or bids reflecting a bargain struck for consideration. That objective of Articles 145, that is somewhat latent in the formulation of the Article in the Constitution, becomes clear upon a perusal of the corresponding Article 299(1) of the Constitution of India which expressly refers to "contracts and all assurances of property" made in the exercise of the power derived from the President. It is evident that Article 299(1) of the Indian Constitution and Article 145(1) of the Constitution have been enacted primarily to guard against avoidable and unwelcome demands made on the treasury pursuant to commercial transactions, the Indian Supreme Court in West Bengal vs BK Mondal & Sons reported in AIR 1962 (SC) 779 held that Article 299(1) of the Indian Constitution has been incorporated on the ground of public policy to protect the state from the liability to unauthorized contracts and, therefore, its provisions are mandatory and non-compliance with its requirements renders a contract invalid and unenforceable. Even so, Mr Mahmudul Islam in his book "Constitutional Law of Bangladesh" (Second Edition: Mullick Brothers, Dhaka 2003) in discussing the ratio on the West Bengal Case in conjunction with Article 145 compliance measures finds, the India Supreme Court's view "too rigid" as it "goes beyond the necessity of protecting the public interest". The better view, according to Mr Islam is that expounded by the Privy Council in Montreal Street Railway Co vs Normandin reported in AIR 1917 PC. 142 that strict compliance in such cases is not to be mandatory and is to be forgone in favour of substantial compliance especially if a strict compliance test declaring a contract null and void would operate to the prejudice of all and sundry. This Court finds that if, therefore, the rigidity of the application of the Article 145(1) conditions are relaxed with regards to contracts and deeds clearly falling under the said Article's purview, there is no reason why a stricter test of validity should be applied to the Peace Accord which, in this Court's view, does not answer to the description of an Article 145(1) contract or deed in the first place. This Court, therefore, notes that when an argument of substantial compliance with the requirements of Article 145(1) can be made with regard to contracts and deeds clearly envisaged in the said Article, the Petitioners in both the Writ Petitions have not satisfactorily explained why the same provisions should be found to be of mandatory application with regard to the Peace Accord which, in our view, is not an Article 145(1) contract: or deed. This Court, therefore, finds that the multi-dimensional Peace Accord does not permit of a neat categorization under the Constitution. Being an essential link in a long-standing and ongoing political process this intrastate peace pact between belligerents is not strictly contemplated for in our Constitution and must, therefore, be found to be indeterminable as to its nature and validity by reference to the Constitution. It is here that we find the relevance of and the merit in Dr Kamal Hossain's submission that the Constitution indeed lacks in process formulation and the CHT peace process with the Peace Accord as its vital component, therefore, considered on their own do not indeed permit a constitution-al analysis adopting a strict constructionist approach. In a similar vein Mr Devasish Roy appearing for the Respondent Regional Council has argued to this Court's satisfaction that the CHT Peace Accord is neither an executive deed nor a contract within the meaning of Article 145, but is merely a political document agreement setting out the political goodwill between the NCCHT negotiating on behalf of the Government and the PCJSS representatives of the tribal people to bring an end to the armed hostility in the CHT. It is further submitted that it is in that spirit of political engagement and accommodation that the Peace Accord was negotiated and executed by the then Chief Whip Mr Abul Hasnat Abdullah in 1997, it always being the intention of both parties concerned to accept him as representing the Government of Bangladesh in that exercise. 

 31. There are other features of the Peace Accord as pointed out by Mr Roy that in this Court's opinion, further learned support to the view that the Peace Accord was not intended to be an end in itself but merely a means to an end. The prime indicator of such status of the Peace Accord is that it was not deemed necessary to subject it to a process of constitutional entrenchment. It is also markedly deficient in having any built-in-safeguards or penalties for its non-compliance as would have positively deterred non-implementation by the Government. Nor does it provide for a quid pro quo arrangement and concomitant carrying out of mutual obligations. It is possible that these aspects of compliance and implementation were left outstanding for future consideration in the interests of securing political benefits in the short run. Given that scenario it is also not surprising that the Peace Accord's provisions on implementation and specific time frame are few and rather vague. In other words, the Peace Accord was clearly never intended to be the preeminent piece of legal document affecting the rights and interests of the parties thereto. It is evident, that such purpose and objective was to be served by the various legislation premised purpose and objective was to be served by the various legislation premised on the Peace Accord with the responsibility, thereby, squarely placed on the Legislature to frame laws as would secure the implementation of the Peace Accord within the constitutional frame work. It would now be for this Court to more appropriately probe into the extent to which the Legislature may have either discharged or abdicated its responsibility in that regard. In this regard, before we proceed on to examining the validity of the amendments introduced by the Impugned Acts of 1998 pertaining to the three District Councils and the one piece of legislation being Act No. 12 of 1998 establishing the Regional Council there is the matter of autonomy of the CHT that this Court has to address. 

 32. The learned Advocate for the Petitioner in Writ Petition No. 6451 of 2007 Mr Moudud Ahmed has in placing his submissions drawn this Court's attention to the history of accommodation that has been pursued by successive regimes in Bangladesh vis-a-vis the CHT up until 1997. Referring extensively to the book, authored by him entitled "South Asia: Crisis of Development—The Case of Bangladesh," Mr Ahmed has shown that successive elected and non-elected governments during that period had pursued in varied degrees policies aimed at the integration of the tribal people of the CHT in the mainstream population and the preferred mechanism for this was development activities and programmes undertaken as part of a larger political solution. The objective was to ensure, according to Mr Ahmed, the peaceful coexistence of the tribal and non-tribal peoples, allowing nevertheless the former their entitlement to preserve their own way of life and culture. It is with that guiding philosophy that two accords prior to the Peace Accord of 1997 were entered into and which, as part of an ongoing process, yielded the three Hill District Local Government Council Acts of 1989. Mr Ahmed has argued by reference to the said three legislation of 1989, as later fell to be amended in 1998, that these had successfully reflected a consensus at bringing about a structural change for maximum self-rule within the framework of a sovereign unitary State. Among the salient features of the laws was to ensure that the complexion of the local government bodies or councils would be such as dominated by the tribal peoples while ensuring proportionate representation of both tribal and non-tribal on the basis of universal adult franchise. Among the functions assigned to the District Councils was that of maintaining law and order, co-ordination of development activities of each district and to engage in a host of activities necessary for the improvement of the tribal areas. Each Council had reserved to itself the authority to approve or not any transfer or settlement of any land within each district and, in particular, with regard to such transfer or settlement favoring any person not permanent resident of the district. Mr Ahmed has argued that these enactments could have indeed continued to well serve the aspiration for autonomy within the framework of the Constitution and, hereby, obviated the necessity to enact the impugned laws of 1998. He has submitted that the philosophy that underpins and informs the Impugned Acts of 1998 in one of recognizing and institutionalizing two distinct classes or categories of citizens within the CHT, namely tribal and non-tribal, with rights, privileges and obligations different from each other. Mr Ahmed submits that such laws as are inherently discriminatory between citizens of the same country are in violation of the guarantees of equality under Articles 27 and 31 of the Constitution. That philosophy, Mr Ahmed contends, has progressed on to a higher plane of administrative and geographical segregation aimed at a probable political detachment of the CHT as a region from the otherwise unitary political fabric of Bangladesh by the enactment of the Regional Council Act (Act No. 12 of 1998). If the objective of this piece of legislation is to enable the Regional Council to propagate the idea of 'self-determination' as distinct from 'self-governance' and to function to that end as a "higher executive authority" over the entire CHT, with that region being taken as a single administrative and political unit, then the Regional Council's operating on that higher plane is argued by Mr Moudud Ahmed to be in violation of Articles 1 and 7 of the Constitution threatening the very concept of the basic unitary structure of the Constitution. Having so heard Mr Ahmed, this Court observes that the integrationist approach actively pursued by the Government at least up until 1989 before being replaced by a rival approach as recognizes the right of tribal people to exist as distinct peoples, almost, in the view of this Court, parallels a similar paradigm shift noted to have taken place at about the same time on the international plane. It is noted in this regard that the ILO Convention on Indigenous and Tribal Populations, 1957 (Convention No. 107) and its accompanying Recommendation No. 104 were adopted in 1957. Up until 1989 this "seminal instrument" is said to have "remained unique in international law as the only comprehensive international statement of the rights of indigenous and tribal population and of the duties of states toward them from 1957 until 1989 "(As per Lee Swepston, "A New Step in the International law on Indigenous and Tribal Peoples: ILO Convention No. 169 of 1989" in Oklahoma City University Law Review, Vol.15, Fall 1990, Number 3, pp.677-714, as quoted by Raja Devasish Roy in "The ILO 'Convention on Indigenous and Tribal Populations, 1957 (No. 107) and The Laws of Bangladesh : A Comparative Review", PRO 169, International Labour Standards Department, ILO Geneva and ILO Office in Dhaka, 2009 page 1). Convention No. 107 is said to have, however, reflected the "mainstream' ideas of the time" in that it sought merely "to provide basic safe-guard measures for indigenous and tribal population groups." (Ibid, Roy, 1). It is noted that Convention No. 107 was ratified by Bangladesh in 1972. It appears, however, according to Devilish Roy in his 2009 ILO publication that the integrationist approach underlining Convention No. 107 was considered to be "patronizing" and "Paternalistic" as is it presupposes that indigenous and tribal peoples shall be way of natural progression and as a consequence of effective participation in the national polity wholly assimilate with and disappear into the mainstream socio-politico-cultural structure thereby irreversibly losing their sense of separateness. The ILO is subsequently said to have subscribed to the more progressive approach of recognizing the indigenous and tribal groups' entitlement to self-identification and ensure their empowerment to that effect in order that they may exist as distinct peoples should they so wish. The paradigm shift is notably reflected in the adoption of the ILO Convention on Indigenous and Tribal Peoples of 1989 (Convention No. 169) as serves as a review of ILO Convention No. 107. Consequentially, as Devasish Roy writes, presently. 

 33. In keeping with the preliminary Rule issued in Writ Petition 2669 of 2000 we now embark on the exercise of determining the constitutionality of the various provisions of the three Hill District Council Acts, of 1989 as amended by the Impugned Acts of 1998 and the Regional Council Act of 1998. Beginning with the Regional Council Act of 1998 considered in its entirety we proceed on the submissions on behalf of the Respondents that the CHT Regional Council being a creation of the Act itself falls within the four corners of the definition of a statutory public authority. It is categorically asserted that the Regional Council does not proclaim to be a local government body itself rather its purpose is to coordinate and supervise the activities of the local government bodies in the CHT in order to present a common forum for addressing common issues in the CHT. In that light it has been argued on behalf of the Respondents that the Regional Council Act facilitates a better functioning by the local government bodies at the district level and in that sense promotes the purpose of Articles 59 and 60 of the Constitution. An examination of that line of argument, this Court hastens to add, would also necessarily require an examination of the definition of what constitutes an administrative unit for the purpose of Article 59 and as found interpreted in Article 152(1) of the Constitution. That brings into focus the counter argument of the Petitioner in Writ Petition No. 2669 of 2000 that the Regional Council created by the Regional Council Act of 1998 has instead all the characteristics of a local government body but at the same time fails to comply with Article 59 of the Constitution. In other words, while operating in the guise of a local government body, its operations vis-à-vis the CHT is unconstitutional given that the CHT has not been declared as an administrative unit for the purposes of Articles 59 read together with Article 152(1). In this regard, the learned Advocate for the Petitioner Mr Abdur Razzaq has argued that local governments under Article 59 have to be setup in administrative units defined under Article 152(1) of the Constitution as a "district or other area designated by law for the purposes of Article 59." Mr Razzaq points out that the CHT, comprising of Rangamati, Khagrachari and Bandarban is not a district, but a combination of three districts. He argues that the CHT has not been designated by any provision of the Regional Council Act as an 'administrative unit' and as such the Regional Council cannot be said to be a local government in an administrative unit for the purposes of Article 59. That argument, in the view of this Court, has to be tested against the ratio of the judgment in Kudrat-e-Elahi Panir vs Bangladesh reported in 44 DLR (AD) 319 in general and primarily against two dicta pronounced by two judges of the Appellate Division in that case. It would stand to reason to refer first to the following observation of Mustafa Kamal J at paragraph 67 at page 341: 

 “……..the words 'Local Government' have not been defined in the Constitution, nor does the Constitution require any organ of the State to create a new local government In the absence of any definition and in the absence of any directive to create a local government afresh, the Constitution will be presumed to have referred to the already-known concept and institution of and the existing legislation on local government. Local government, as a concept and as an institution, was already known to have possessed certain common characteristics namely, local elections, procedure for public accountability, independent and substantial sources of income, clear areas for independent action and certainty of powers and duties and the conditions under which they would be exercised." 

 The above observation and finding must necessarily be considered in the context of the interpretation given to the words "administration unit" in Article 152(1) of the Constitution as meaning "a district or other area designated by law for the purposes of article 59" of the Constitution. It is also noted that Mostafa Kamal J's observation above came to be reinforced by that of Shahabuddin Ahmed CJ in the Kudrat-e-Elahi Panir case when he latter at paragraph 20 at page 330 said that local government "is meant for management of local affairs by local elected persons." 

 34. It is against such judicial dicta that this Court has perused the Regional Council Act (Act No. 12 of 1998) and that exercise reveals that the Regional Council prima facie exhibits all the characteristics of local governments as identified in the Kudrat-e-Elahi Panir case. Thus, for example, sections 20 and 21 of that Regional Council Act provide for local elections and, as submitted by Mr. Abdur Razzaq, by extension public accountability. Sections 32(Kha) 4 (Gha) (Umo) and (Cha) provide for independent sources of fund/income of the Regional Council. Section 22 provides for clear areas for independent action by the Regional Council and in a manner that these can be discharged relatively free from governmental influence and interference. Therefore, tested against Shahabuddin Ahmed CJ's enunciation above, Mr. Abdur Razzaq sees the Regional Council Act as envisaging administration of local affairs by locally elected persons, through the agency and forum of the Regional Council, and, as such, the same as being intended to function as a local government within the meaning of Article 59. It is on the basis of the above that Mr. Abdur Razzaq has argued that under the Regional Council Act, to all intents and purposes, the Regional Council is envisaged as a local government body within the meaning of Article 59. He thereafter, proceeds to conclude that in view of the fact the Regional Council comprises of elected representatives of the CHT region and exhibits all the characteristics of a local government, it was incumbent upon the Legislature to designate the CHT region as an administrative unit for the purposes of Article 59. The Legislature having evidently failed to do so, the submission now is that entire Regional Council Act is, therefore, unconstitutional. 

 35. A reading of Articles 59 and 60 with Article 152(1) makes it evident to this court that local governments under Article 59 have indeed to be set up in administrative units defined in Article 152(1) either as a district or any other area designated by law for the purposes of Article 59. It is clear as well that the CHT, comprising of Rangamati, Khagrachari and Bandarban, is not a district, but a composite of these three districts with the said districts compositely being referred to as a 'region'. In that light a perusal of Regional Council Act does not, however, reveal any designation of the CHT region as an administrative unit. The essentiality of such designation as contemplated in the scheme of the Constitution has been clearly subscribed to, developed and entrenched by the judgment in the Kudrat-e-Elahi Panir Case as subsequently also referred to, for example, in the judgment in BLAST vs Bangladesh. reported in 60 DLR 234. In the Kudrat-e- Elahi Panir case, Shahabuddin Ahmed CJ at paragraph 29 in no uncertain terms declared the necessity of such designation thus: 

 "For true construction of Article 152(1) defining an 'administrative unit' the primary rule of construction will be sufficient in this case. In this Article the words "district or any other area" are to be read conjunctively, and if is done, a "district" is found to be an administrative unit, and for the purpose of Article 59, that is to say, for establishing a Local Government there, no designation by law is necessary. But as  regards "any other area" it will be an  "Administrative unit" only if it is specifically designated as such by law." 

 36. It is at this juncture that this Court has taken into consideration Mr Abdur Razzaq's submission that the Regional Court has assumed the complexion of a local government body, and that too an elected one, without express designation of the CHT region as an administrative unit within which the Council otherwise purports to exercise authority in local governance. In this context Mr Razzaq has drawn this Court's attention to Article 59(2) of the Constitution that lists among the possible functions of local government bodies those as may be prescribed by Act of Parliament and which may include functions relating to administration, maintenance of public order, and the preparation and implementation of plans relating to public services and economic development. But reference to that list of functions in Article 59(2) we find neatly tucked way in the crevices of section 22 of the Regional Council Act, that section otherwise, being generally declaratory of the power of supervision and coordination vested in the Regional Council the following provision of section 22(Gha), in particular, that reads thus: পার্বত্য জেলার সাধারণ প্রশাসন, আইন শৃঙ্খলা ও উন্নয়নের তত্বাবধান ও সমন্বয় সাধন।It is this Court's view, that the said provision in one HC-71 sweeping stroke wholly undermines the argument on behalf of the Respondents highlighting the functions of the Regional Council as a mere facilitator acting in a supervisory and coordinating capacity. We are in these circumstances inclined to find that the Regional Council comprising locally elected person and entrusted with the management of local affairs was designed and intended, but without a prior designation of the CHT region as an "administration unit", to operate is a local government body and the mere fact that the Regional Council had additionally been entrusted with the powers of supervision and coordination. does not take it outside of the fold of local government. To paraphrase the finding in the BLAST case as above referred, the Regional Council has been clothed with all the powers and functions of a local government body, it has all the attributes of such a body but its status in this regard as a local government body, absent an express designation of its territorial operational base, i.e., the CHT as an administrative unit, appear to have been "purposefully shield-ed." The conclusion as shall inevitably have to be drawn from the above is that Regional Council Act is nothing but a mere colorable piece of legislation and must on this ground alone by struck down as being ultra virus of the Constitution. In arriving at this finding, this Court has also considered a related aspect/feature in the Regional Council Act, which gives further credence to the unconstitutionality of the said Act. This has to do with the provisions of sections 40 and 41 of the Regional Council Act as reproduced herein below: 

 37. This Court finds that section 40(2) and section 41 read together leads to the unavoidable conclusion that constitutional violations as envisaged under section 40(2) will not necessarily in the scheme of the Regional Council Act lead to a termination or dissolution of the Regional Council. This, we note, appears to authorize the Regional Council to operate in derogation of the Constitution with a considerable degree of impunity. Mr Razzaq has submitted that this gives us a grandstand view of a full-frontal attack on the Constitution and, reflects furthermore a stepping stone to the dismantling of the unitary character of the State. Prior to addressing that particular scenario, suffice it to state at this juncture that for all of Mr Razzaq's arguments pertaining to the unconstitutionality of the Peace Accord and the consequential legislation in particular, nowhere is his submission that there has been a fraud on the Constitution better substantiated in this Court's view that in this instance. Mr Razzaq has further pointed out that for all its textual incongruities as has the effect of equalizing, if not demoting, the status of the Constitution vis-a-vis the Regional Council Act, section 40(2) is also notably silent on any sanction or consequence that shall befall the Regional Council should it upon a constitutional infraction not pay heed to the advice proffered by the Government to mend its ways in that regard. This Court has pondered whether section 41 of the Act as deals with grounds for the dissolution of the Regional Council devises a sanction in such a circumstance. Mr Razzaq submits that section 41 is of no assistance in that regard on account of being inadequately drafted. He has drawn our attention to section 41(1)(Gha) which in its generality of formulation is expressly different from the specific grounds stipulated in section 41(1)(Ka), (Kha) and (Ga) and can by the application of the principle of ejusdem generis be read as incorporating provisions of a genre different from those otherwise found preceding it is section 41(1). Mr Razzaq has submitted that section 41(1)(Gha) in particular and section 41 in general, and the cause for upholding the supremacy of the Constitution under Act No.  12 of 1998, would have been better served should the reference to "the Constitution” in section 40 have been matched by an equally express reference to 'the Constitution' in section 41(1), thereby allowing for its violation to be a ground for termination or dissolution of the Council. But that clearly has not been done. This Court is now reminded there of the judgment in Bangladesh vs Abdul Mannan reported in 29 DLR (SC) 17 for its express reliance on the maxim 'Expressio unius est exclusion alterius', that is, express mention of one thing implies the exclusion of other things. From a reading of the Regional Council Act in particular this Court holds that this omission in section 41 of the Act actually reflects the legislative intent of deliberate excluding that which has not been declared or referred to in the Act. In light of that finding of deliberate exclusion, this Court has taken note of the admission by the learned Attorney General Mr Mahbubey Alam that section 40 as permits constitutional infractions with impunity is indeed incongruous with the overall scheme of the Regional Council Act as interpreted by him, and that to that extent the said formulation of section 40 must be accepted as the product of a bona fide legislative error and, consequentially, there is fact remains to cause for the reference to the term 'Constitution' or `704M' to remain in the body of section 40(2). We are, however, inclined not to accept that line of argument given that sections 40 and 41 appear to be deliberate in their formulation to further the underlying cause of the Regional Council Act to erode the unitarily of the State. The Regional Council Act, this Court notes, is therefore aptly perceived by the Petitioner to undermine and endanger the unitary character of the State as otherwise enshrined in Article I of the Constitution and manifesting, thereby, a basic feature of the Constitution. 

 39.
