The Petitioner in Writ Petition No. 2669 of 2000 has submitted by reference to various local government legislations like the Zilla Parishad Ain, 2000, Upazilla Parishad Act, 1998, the Local Government (Paurashava) Act, 2009, the Local Government (Union) Paris had Act 2009, and the Local Government (City Corporation) Act, of 2009 that provisions in these legislation allowing for extensive control, supervision and inquiry into the affairs of the local government bodies by the Executive are simply absent in the three Hill District Council Acts as amended. In fact, the three Hill District Councils are submitted to be the only local government bodies that enjoy freedom from the control and supervision of the Executive and this is further bolstered by the fact that the new section 50 of the three Hill District Council Acts merely allows the Government to issue non-binding recommendations and directions upon the three Councils with no consequences further provided for the failure of the three Hill District Councils to implement the same. It is also pointed out that section 53 of the, three Hill District Council Acts and the powers conferred there under cannot be invoked to dissolve any such Council in the event of a failure to implement such non-binding recommendations of the Government. Such a lax regulatory frame-work, it is submitted, is intended to remove any real scope of control by the Executive, thereby, providing greater autonomy to the Hill people in terms of self-governance. 

 44. Upon a consideration of the above, this Court has, however, deemed it prudent to peruse certain other provisions being sections 12, 20, 43 and 55 of the there Original Acts that read collective, in our view, do go a certain length to in fact consolidate the Government's authority in the local governance function of the said three administrative units. This we see as an attempt of strike a real and essential balance between the powers of the Executive and the authority and privileges of the local government units that creates a healthy atmosphere aiding the achievement of democratic governance in the three Hill districts. Therefore, considered within this broader scheme of the Original Acts, there is nothing found in sections 50 and 53 that in the view of .this Court has the potential of ushering in autonomy in its broader sense as an expression of self-determination and on that ground this Court is now disinclined to interfere with these provisions being sections 50 and 53 of the three Hill District Council Acts. 

 46. Against that backdrop, section 6 of the 1998 Acts as amending section 4 of the 1989 Acts endorsing the authority of a Circle Chief, on the basis of a certificate issued by the head-man of the village, to decide whether a person is a non-tribal or not appears indeed to contravene the provisions of Articles 27, 28(1), 29(1), and 31 of the Constitution on the fundamental ground that the 1989 Acts as amended provide on further objective yardstick against which .a decision to grant or not such a certificate may be measured. The same provisions of the Constitution are validly submitted to invalidate the provisions of section 17 of the 1989 Acts as amended by section 11 of 1998 as requires a person to be both an owner of land in the CHT as well a permanent resident in order to vote in the local government council elections. That in this Court's view has the practical effect of denying a non-tribal citizen to be a voter in any election in CHT whereas he has reserved to him the right to do so anywhere else in Bangladesh under the Constitution. 

 47. It is noted further that the provisos to section 32(2) and 62(1) of the 1989 Acts as amended in 1998 now allow for preference to be given the tribals both for employment in the Hill District Councils as well as the Police Force. Thus, the requirement of a preferential treatment has been introduced notably in lieu of requirement of proportional representation that previously governed both the provisions. Here as well, in the absence of any indication in the Acts as to how and on what objective basis an individual shall be the beneficiary of such a preferential treatment to the detriment and exclusion of another, this Court is now inclined to hold that these provisions sanctioning arbitrary selection are in contravention of Article 27, 28(1), 29(1) and (2) and 31 of the Constitution. In this regard, the absence of such objective standards especially invalidate the introductions by amendment of the notion of preferential treatment' and render these unconstitutional given that it endorses discrimination on grounds of race etc. It will be prudent, how-ever, to note in this regard that the rule-making authority of the Government under section 68 of the 1989 Acts ought to have been actively exercised by the Government by now to over-come the objections raised with regard to the continued of such of the above-referred provisions of the 1989 Acts as have been found by this Court to be in violation of Article 27, 28(1), 29(1) and (2), and 31 of the Constitution. The fact that section 89 as provides for such rule-making authority, now in its amended form, has introduced an element of consultation by the Government with the concerned District Council with the authority reserved to the latter to review and modify any Government propos-al as to the formulation of such rules does not, in our view, of itself prevent the formulation of comprehensive and effective rules per se. There is no information available to this Court at the present time as to whether any rules at all have been framed and put into affect under the common section 68 of Acts of 1989. 

 48. Of the two outstanding objections of the petitioner in writ petition No 2669 of 2000 with regard to the provisions of the Acts of 1989 as amended in 1998, the first has to do with the fact of the removal or deletion of the words 'Local Government' from the entire text of these three original acts and the petitioner's submission that such deletion must be tested against the legislative truism that parliament not being in the practice to do or say anything in vain the deletion of the words 'Local Government' therefore, ought not be considered without any significance. In this regard, the Petitioner has emphasized such significance to lie in the contest of such deletion being in contravention of Article 59 of the Constitution in particular. Considered on its own such deletion appears fairly innocuous to this Court given the fact that any district council squarely falls within the ambit of the definition of an administrative unit under Article 152(1) of the Constitution, and should all the other requirements of the law in establishing such a local government unit be found to be in place, mere absence of a term or two of identification as a 'Local Government' unit will not necessarily detract from the unit's status as an unit of local governance. That test happily applies to the three District Council Acts of 1989 as amended in 1998 and this Court is, therefore, disinclined to interfere with this act of deletion as other-wise prayed for. Furthermore, given that this Court has already found against the validity and legality of the Regional Council Act in its entirety. Thereby, avoiding the possibility of the Regional Council's continued operation potentially encouraging and informing the work of the three District Councils to aim at political and territorial self-determination, the deletion of the words 'Local Government' in the Original Acts proves now to be of no substantive consequence.  49. Both Mr. Abdur Razzaq and one of the Amici Curiae, Mr TH Khan have impressed upon this Court the necessity, at the end of the day, for this Court's intervention in these Applications to be supplemented by the formulation of controlling principles to guide all par-ties to press on with the peace process and ensure its sustainability within the framework of the Constitution. Mr Razzaq, in particular, has drawn this Court's attention to at least one similar exercise undertaken in the Philippines in the case of Province of North Cotabato vs the Government of the Republic of Philippines Peace Panel on Ancestral Domain. Given this Court's views that the CHT peace process to be sustainable must be informed by concerned innovative efforts at constant evaluation and reinvention, the following guidelines are formulated only at indicators of the broad spectrum of issues that will have to bolster the peace and are by no means intended to be exhaustive in their ambit: 

 (a) 	The petitioner in Writ Petition No. 2669 of 2000 somewhat poignantly argued that if this Court in declaring the Regional Council Act to be unconstitutional declines, however, to strike down the Peace Accord, this would result in an anomalous situation with the Government remaining obliged under section 'Gha' of the peace Accord to enact a Regional Council law. It is the finding of this Court that one of the reasons behind this Court's disinclination to interfere with the Peace Accord being the merger of the relevant provisions of the Accord with the impugned legislation, it is to be deduced there from that for all practical purposes the CHT Peace Accord is to be taken to that extent by all concerned to be a spent force and no residual obligation arises under the Accord to legislate afresh on the lines of the Regional Council Act of 1998. Furthermore, any attempt at such legislation shall indeed be in derogation of the findings of this Court. It is noted that the learned Attorney General Mr Mahbubey Alam and Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud as Amici Curiae had argued in favour of the constitutionality of the Regional Council At of 1998 s in their view established a statutory public authority, albeit an elected one, and which was intended to contribute to the process of democratic governance in the three Hill Districts by serving as a conduit between the Government in Dhaka and the three local governments units at the district level. This Court having, however, found the Regional Council Act to be lacking the those features, opines that it would nevertheless remain open for the Government as part of the ongoing peace process to form a statutory pubic authority comprising wholly of nominated members to serve the purpose of a facilitator to local governance and to act as a conduit, as the Regional Council may otherwise have ideally accomplished within the bounds of the Constitution, and possessed of the features as sub-mitted by both Mr Alam and Mr Mahmud. 

 (b) 	It has not escaped this Court's attention that the peace process has not been served well by inordinate delay in its full implementation and that time has not indeed been kind to the peace process. The present fractious, volatile and the deeply entrenched and polarized political situation in the CHT amply attest to that. It is certainly an irony that the peace process as aims at democratic governance has not thus far been able to ensure the practice of democracy in the CHT to any discernibly commendable extent. One of the best possible ways for the local government or District Councils to have been actively engaged in the management of their own affairs was to have regular elections to the District Councils that would not only have strengthened participatory politics as well as the process of integration of the peoples of the CHT, but would have been an antidote to anarchy and defused the power of anarchic forces. It is this Court's considered view that democratic governance by the active exercise of participatory politics in the three Hill Districts is and always will be the lifeblood of the peace process and should be encouraged and pursued in all earnest. 

 (c) 	Much has been said by way of sub-missions before this Court not only with regard to the recognition of back-ward sections of citizens but also with regard to the mode, manner and process of identifying such backwardness. While it is true that the history of the CHT attests to relative backwardness of that part of the country in terms of certain identifiable criteria pertaining to communication, nonagricultural and, education, health and sanitation, annual per capital income, availability of pain land etc., it is also evident that these criteria have not been resolved upon as the fully governing criteria objectively identified, evaluated and assessed to sustain claims for continued positive legislative interventions under Articles 28(4) and 29(3) of  the Constitution., There are examples in other jurisdictions of commissions or bodies set up at national level to ascertain and determine backwardness on the basis of reliable and quantifiable data premised on which any government can validly justify its identification of one group or the order over its other citizens to be backward and therefore, to be entitled to the positive discriminatory measures adopted by legislation. This is all the more imperative in our jurisdiction given that the Constitution itself does not prescribe the procedure, method or mechanism of identification of backward sections of citizens and it being inadvisable for this Court to lay down any such procedure, method or, mechanism in that constitutional vacuum. That responsibility in these circumstances lies squarely with the Government itself which can adopt such method and procedure, as it deems reasonable and convenient to that end. It is not that governmental action in this area is wholly without precedence in Bangladesh. This Court has taken note of the work already done by the Ministry for CHT Affairs in 2008 as referred to above and which may very well serve as a base reference for any future endeavour in this area of enquiry. 

 (d) 	As Mr TH Khan has stressed and impressed upon this Court, prudence and pragmatism dictates that the Government press on with the peace process against the backdrop of a larger geo-strategic context given, in particular, the history and the regional setting under which the conflict in the CHT arose, was sustained and which at one stage in the peace process was brought to an end with the signing of the Peace Accord in 1997.
